text:
Ahead of Thanksgiving, more Americans struggle to put food on the table
Rising costs of groceries, housing and gas have pushed more people to seek emergency food assistance
Andreas Leal and his wife peruse the shelves at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas. Food banks and pantries across the country are experiencing surging demand amid declining federal food assistance and higher grocery prices. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)
KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards.
As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and the hodgepodge of donated items on the toiletry shelves. A 75-year-old retiree, Leal said every bit helps when trying to keep up with rising prices.
“It’s very expensive,” he said. “Everything is expensive right now.”
Leal said his monthly Social Security benefit can’t keep up with rising costs. While the federal program boosted benefits by 2.8% this year, he said he just received notice that his residential property tax bill will jump 30%, costing him some $600. The increases require constant trade-offs. For example, to save on gas, the couple forgoes trips to visit their son who lives about 45 minutes away.
Leaders of Cross-Lines Community Outreach say such stories are more and more common. Its Community Market, a food pantry resembling a grocery store, serves about 1,900 families per month — a 35% increase over last year.
“Daily, we have to turn people away,” said Executive Director Susila Jones.
The market previously aimed to provide a couple pounds of frozen ground beef each month to every family. But those costs are now too high, pushing Cross-Lines to buy ground turkey or chicken — if prices are low enough.
Cross-Lines serves people across Wyandotte County, one of the most populous counties in Kansas with a poverty rate that exceeds state and national averages. In recent years, the food pantry has become more lenient about its income requirements and welcomed people who seek aid from multiple organizations.
“This is not what people want to do and so we really just let people come to us when they need to come to us,” she said. “Because we know even if you are working, if you’ve had steady income, just one paycheck can put you over the edge.”
Rising costs of groceries, housing and gas have pushed more people to seek emergency food assistance. At the same time, those charitable organizations are seeing a wave of Americans who have lost access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, the nation’s largest food assistance program.

title: Woman accused in Nampa crash that killed mother, newborn gets trial date
summary: ‼️A March trial date has been set for the woman charged in connection with a Nampa crash that killed a 19-year-old mother and her newborn daughter.
text:
NAMPA, Idaho — A trial date has been set for Abigail Nicole Wolverton, the woman charged in connection with a Nampa crash that killed a 19-year-old mother and her newborn daughter.
Wolverton appeared in Canyon County court on Tuesday, where her trial was set to begin March 1, 2027.
RELATED | $2 million bond set for Nampa woman arrested for aggravated DUI, injury to child
Wolverton faces two counts of aggravated vehicular manslaughter and one count of injury to a child.
The charges stem from an Aug. 31 crash at Middleton Road and Lake Lowell Avenue in Nampa.
Kyara Engelhart, 19, was eight months pregnant when she was seriously injured in the crash.
Doctors performed an emergency C-section. Engelhart died Sept. 3, and her newborn daughter, Maelynn Lindauer, died Sept. 7.
RELATED | 19-year-old mother, newborn daughter die after Nampa DUI crash; charges amended
Wolverton is being held on a $2 million bond. The case is scheduled to go to trial March 1, 2027.
For Canyon County happenings, news, and more— join our Facebook Group: 2C Neighborhood News - Nampa, Caldwell, Middleton
This story was initially reported by a journalist and has been, in part, converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

title: Human rights groups sue ICE alleging detention of pregnant, nursing immigrants
summary: The Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and several other groups filed a lawsuit Tuesday against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement alleging that the agency is illegally detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants against its own policies. The suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the […]
text:
Human rights groups sue ICE alleging detention of pregnant, nursing immigrants
Lawsuit cites 2021 ICE directive, which states agents shouldn’t ‘detain, arrest, or take into custody’ anyone who is known to be pregnant, postpartum or nursing
Federal immigration officers are shown at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in March. A lawsuit filed by advocacy organizations alleges the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is violating a 2021 directive by detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing women. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)
The Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and several other groups filed a lawsuit Tuesday against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement alleging that the agency is illegally detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants against its own policies.
The suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, cites a 2021 ICE directive, which states that agents “should not detain, arrest, or take into custody for an administrative violation” anyone who is known to be pregnant, postpartum or nursing.
According to the complaint, ICE has stopped tracking the number of women who are pregnant, postpartum or nursing and being held in detention under the Trump administration. But one of the plaintiff organizations — the Women’s Refugee Commission — obtained data through a Freedom of Information Act request. Those documents showed an increase of pregnant women in ICE detention between January 2025 and March 2026 from nine to 128, or a 1,320% increase, the complaint states.
The length of detention for pregnant women has also increased substantially, according to the complaint.
“Since 2025, ICE detained more than 557 pregnant women for an average of 43 days,” the complaint reads. “Nearly 14% of these women were detained for 90 days or longer, with one woman detained for 219 days, almost seven months of her pregnancy.”
A spokesperson from the Department of Homeland Security said in an email sent to Stateline that the 2021 directive is still in place, and that pregnancy in ICE detention is “exceedingly rare,” making up 0.15% of all of those currently in custody as of Oct. 31.
The spokesperson said pregnant women in detention receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, nutritional support and other accommodations.
“This includes medical, dental, and mental health intake screening within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility, a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arrival at a facility, and access to necessary medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care,” the statement said. “This is the best healthcare many of these individuals have received in their entire lives.”

title: Turkey production bounces back but prices still rise
summary: Turkey production for Thanksgiving has increased this year for the first time since avian diseases reduced supplies for years, but prices still rose as labor shortages created bottlenecks, according to federal reports. Turkey farmers, like other livestock producers, say they need more foreign workers as immigration crackdowns and the ending of protected status for many […]
text:
Turkey production bounces back but prices still rise
Turkey farmers, like other livestock producers, say they need more foreign workers as immigration crackdowns limit workforce
Turkeys gather for feeding at Whiffletree Farm in Virginia in September. Turkey production is up this year after two years of decline but prices rose because of strong demand and a shortage of whole birds. (Photo courtesy of Whiffletree Farm)
Turkey production for Thanksgiving has increased this year for the first time since avian diseases reduced supplies for years, but prices still rose as labor shortages created bottlenecks, according to federal reports.
Turkey farmers, like other livestock producers, say they need more foreign workers as immigration crackdowns and the ending of protected status for many immigrants take a toll on their workforce. Many producers support proposed bipartisan federal legislation to give them more access to visas for temporary workers.
Disruptions to Temporary Protected Status for some immigrants “could create significant operational challenges and further tighten an already constrained labor market,” Leslee Oden, CEO of the National Turkey Federation, wrote in an October op-ed supporting the federal visa legislation.
“This is a good first step to help packers and processors keep the rural economy moving and to ensure American consumers have access to affordable food,” Meat Institute CEO Julie Anna Potts said in a statement earlier this year.
Minnesota, North Carolina and Arkansas last year had the highest turkey production numbers, and millions of turkeys were also produced in Indiana, Iowa, Missouri, Pennsylvania and Virginia, according to a U.S. Department of Agriculture report.
Wholesale prices shot up to a projected $1.76 a pound for whole hen turkeys this year from $1.36 last year and just 94 cents in 2024, according to the USDA, a 30% one-year increase. But a Farm Bureau report found retail prices for turkey up only about 10% from last year as retailers used turkey promotions to draw customers – some reported prices as low as 69 cents per pound.
Production increased this year to 5.1 billion pounds, after dropping two years in a row to as low as 4.8 billion pounds last year, but it’s still well below 2020’s 5.7 billion, according to the USDA report.
“They’ve had a lot of disease pressure over the years, so they’re still building up production numbers. That being said, grocery stores love to offer turkey deals,” said Farm Bureau Deputy Chief Economist Faith Parum in a November podcast.
Jesse Straight, who sells about 1,000 turkeys a year directly to customers at his Whiffletree Farm in Warrenton, Virginia, said he hasn’t been as affected by labor and disease issues as other, larger operations. His birds live outside on pastures with more fresh air than factory farms, and he pays a small staff fair wages, he said.

title: Newborn vaccination rates for hepatitis B drop sharply
summary: The percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccine has declined sharply in recent years, falling to 65.6% in June 2026 from 79.8% in 2022, according to a new study published Nov. 24 in the New England Journal of Medicine. The authors of the peer-reviewed study looked at health records from more than 1.3 million […]
text:
Newborn vaccination rates for hepatitis B drop sharply
New study shows vaccine rates for newborns falling to 65.6% in June 2026, down from 79.8% in 2022
A worker applies an adhesive bandage to a child at a vaccination clinic in Minneapolis’ Corcoran Park in August 2023. A new study found the nationwide percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccination has declined sharply since 2023. (Photo courtesy of the City of Minneapolis)
The percentage of newborns receiving the hepatitis B vaccine has declined sharply in recent years, falling to 65.6% in June 2026 from 79.8% in 2022, according to a new study published Nov. 24 in the New England Journal of Medicine.
The authors of the peer-reviewed study looked at health records from more than 1.3 million infants and found that the percentage of babies receiving the hepatitis B vaccination within one day of birth began declining around 2023. The study also found that fewer mothers testing positive for hepatitis B got the vaccine for their babies, from around 98% of those infants in 2025 to around 94% in 2026.
A panel of federal vaccine advisers, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, voted in December 2025 to end the longtime recommendation for infants to receive the hepatitis B vaccination at birth even if the mom tested negative. That decision is on hold pending legal challenges.
The study was based on data from Truveta, a health data and analytics company owned and governed by 30 health systems across the nation.
In explaining the December change, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said screening of pregnant women is highly reliable and can spot disease early. But Nina Masters, an author of the new study and a principal applied research scientist at Truveta specializing in infectious disease and maternal health, told Stateline that “not every mother is tested during pregnancy, and not every person who gets tested has a known status.”
“And screening is imperfect,” she said. “This birth dose has been a universal recommendation to be a safety net to catch those kids that might fall through the cracks, and what we’re seeing here is that that safety net is kind of falling apart.”
Hepatitis B is a contagious liver infection that can cause symptoms of fatigue, loss of appetite and jaundice, and potentially lead to cancer. But it can be prevented through a vaccination. The virus can be passed down from an infected mother to a baby, so since 1991, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recommended that all newborns receive the hepatitis B vaccination within a day after birth to prevent early infections, especially when mothers test positive.
A 2023 study by CDC researchers found that between 1990 and 2019, with the recommendation for newborn vaccination, there was a 99% decline in reported cases of acute hepatitis B among people younger than 19 years old.

summary: On Jan. 1, Idaho families and students will gain access to one of the most exciting educational opportunities in a generation. Thanks to the new federal scholarship tax credit, Idaho taxpayers will be able to direct up to $1,700 of their federal income taxes toward supporting students and schools in their own communities. text:
Two education tax credits, two very different opportunities for Idaho families
Idaho taxpayers will be able to direct up to $1,700 of their federal income taxes toward supporting students and schools here, write guest columnists Terry Ryan and Duncan Robb.
The federal scholarship tax credit is fundamentally different from Idaho’s Parental Choice Tax Credit. While Idaho’s program exclusively benefits private school and homeschool families, the federal scholarship tax credit supports students in public, public charter and private schools, write guest columnists Terry Ryan and Duncan Robb. (Photo by Getty Images)
On Jan. 1, Idaho families and students will gain access to one of the most exciting educational opportunities in a generation.
Thanks to the new federal scholarship tax credit, Idaho taxpayers will be able to direct up to $1,700 of their federal income taxes toward supporting students and schools in their own communities. Money that otherwise would go to Washington, D.C., stays in Idaho to support our schools and families.
This will unlock new resources for student learning, expand educational opportunities, and strengthen Idaho public schools — all at no net cost to participating taxpayers or the state, as we previously wrote, as seen in Idaho Education News.
The federal scholarship tax credit is fundamentally different from Idaho’s Parental Choice Tax Credit. While Idaho’s program exclusively benefits private school and homeschool families, the federal scholarship tax credit supports students in public, public charter and private schools.
Understandably, the two programs have caused some confusion, compounded by recent headlines surrounding an Idaho Tax Commission report on the state program. But the distinctions are significant: the programs differ in how they are funded, who benefits and how the funds can be used.
For starters, the federal scholarship tax credit applies to federal taxes, while Idaho’s Parental Choice Tax Credit applies to state taxes. Passed by the Idaho Legislature in 2024, the state credit took effect this year. The federal program, meanwhile, launches Jan. 1, when taxpayers can begin making qualifying donations and claim their credits when filing federal taxes in 2028 and beyond.
The funding mechanisms also differ significantly. Idaho’s tax credit is funded by a $50 million state appropriation, while the federal program relies entirely on individual and voluntary taxpayer donations to scholarship granting organizations.
Donors receive a federal tax credit for their contributions, and the total scholarship funding available to students depends on how many taxpayers choose to participate each year, effectively making individual Idaho taxpayers philanthropists for schools and students they want to support.
The federal tax credit can and will benefit public school students. In fact, public school is where the lion’s share of the impact will be because most Idaho students attend a public school.

title: Two-thirds of Idaho voters turned out for 2026 general election, final results show
summary: About two-thirds of Idaho’s more than 1 million registered voters cast ballots in the midterm election held earlier this month, according to finalized state election data. The turnout didn’t eclipse rates from 2018, when the governor seat was open without an incumbent, but this year’s election still turned out to be the state’s largest midterm […]
text:
Two-thirds of Idaho voters turned out for 2026 general election, final results show
Idaho’s top election official addressed issues reporting votes in Latah, Bannock counties and long lines in Canyon County
Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at the Calvary Baptist Church in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
About two-thirds of Idaho’s more than 1 million registered voters cast ballots in the midterm election held earlier this month, according to finalized state election data.
The turnout didn’t eclipse rates from 2018, when the governor seat was open without an incumbent, but this year’s election still turned out to be the state’s largest midterm election, with about 734,000 voters showing up, Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane said Tuesday. McGrane, the state’s top election official, attributes that last metric to the state’s years as one of the nation’s fastest growing states.
“It really was a successful election,” McGrane said. “When you think about 734,000 people going through and doing the same thing. That’s a huge Herculean effort.”
Weeks after the Nov. 3 general election, the Idaho State Board of Canvassers on Tuesday certified the results of the election as official. At the board’s meeting at the Idaho State Capitol, officials delved into the results of audits of counties’ election results — including in two counties that underreported votes — and reflected on lessons learned from the election.
The final results showed that no races in Idaho were close enough to warrant a free recount, McGrane said. But he said there still might be a recount in a county assessor race in Shoshone County.
Here’s a few snapshots about how voters turned out to vote earlier this month:
- About 40% of voters didn’t cast ballots at the polls on Election Day. About half of those votes were early in person, for a total of roughly 146,000, and the other half were by absentee ballot, for a total of roughly 145,000. Both of those voting types are becoming more popular, McGrane said.
- Overall, the rate of voters who turned out this year was close to matching the 2018 election, which saw the highest turnout of a midterm election in recent years when nearly 67% of registered voters cast ballots. But this year’s turnout still pales in comparison to years when the president is on the ballot, when an average of nearly 76% of voters show up.
- About 56,000 Idahoans registered to vote on Election Day. McGrane said that might’ve contributed to lines at polling places in some areas. Registering to vote typically takes longer than checking in at the polls.

In North Idaho’s Latah County, where officials announced 2,300 unreported ballots almost a week after the election, McGrane attributed the issue to human error. title: Democrats plan investigations of Trump. Here’s how his Justice Department is fighting back.
summary: As the Trump administration prepares for Democrats to launch an onslaught of investigations in the next Congress, the U.S. Department of Justice is turning to a three-word phrase to preemptively fight back: “Legitimate legislative purpose.” The Justice Department has sent letters in recent days to leading Democratic lawmakers raising the possibility they’ll face criminal prosecution […]
text:
Democrats plan investigations of Trump. Here’s how his Justice Department is fighting back.
DOJ has sent letters to leading Democratic lawmakers raising possibility they’ll face criminal prosecution for conducting aggressive oversight
A banner showing President Donald Trump hangs on the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 20, 2026. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)
As the Trump administration prepares for Democrats to launch an onslaught of investigations in the next Congress, the U.S. Department of Justice is turning to a three-word phrase to preemptively fight back: “Legitimate legislative purpose.”
The Justice Department has sent letters in recent days to leading Democratic lawmakers raising the possibility they’ll face criminal prosecution for conducting aggressive oversight of President Donald Trump and his aides. Legal experts have widely dismissed the threats as empty because the U.S. Constitution affords lawmakers wide protections from prosecution for official actions taken in Congress.
But the letters — and that short phrase within them — offer a blueprint for how the White House will try to undermine the investigations themselves, in addition to discrediting the investigators. Democrats will take control of Congress with majorities in both the House and Senate in early January.
Line of attack
The Justice Department is signaling it will attack congressional subpoenas seeking documents and testimony from federal officials as driven by retribution and outside the bounds of traditional oversight. The government appears ready to argue such requests cross a line into illegality.
The DOJ letters allege Democrats intend to violate federal laws that prohibit individuals acting in an official capacity from violating the constitutional rights of others. In this case, those supposedly having their rights violated would be Trump’s associates.
“As you should know, whatever investigations you and your fellow Democrats have planned must have a legitimate legislative purpose,” U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz, the top Justice Department official in the Southern District of Texas, wrote on Nov. 19 to Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat.
Reitz, a former Republican candidate for Texas attorney general, included similar language in letters to Rep. Robert Garcia and Sen. Adam Schiff of California, Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts. All are Democrats likely to play prominent roles in investigating the Trump administration after the party takes control of Congress in January.
Additionally, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, in a Nov. 9 letter to Garcia wrote that “abusive and capricious threats” were spreading among Democratic legislators. He warned that the Trump administration “will not be extorted” and expected lawmakers to investigate within settled constitutional limits.

title: Trump pardons West Virginia turkeys, Freedom and Feathers
summary: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump pardoned two turkeys named Freedom and Feathers Tuesday, a Thanksgiving White House tradition that dates back to the George H.W. Bush administration. Trump used the brief event on the White House South Lawn to tout renovations, including a new granite helipad and progress on the ballroom, where he said next […]
text:
Trump pardons West Virginia turkeys, Freedom and Feathers
President uses event on White House South Lawn to tout renovations, including new granite helipad and progress on ballroom
President Donald Trump grants a presidential pardon to Freedom, the National Thanksgiving turkey, as, left to right, National Turkey Federation Chairwoman Christy Puffenbarger, first lady Melania Trump and Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., look on during the 79th annual National Thanksgiving Turkey Presentation on the South Lawn of the White House on Nov. 24, 2026 in Washington, D.C. The turkeys, Freedom and Feathers, were raised and trained at Deans Gap Farm in Fort Seybert, West Virginia, by Scott and Becky Rightsell. Freedom and Feathers will retire to Texas A&M University following the ceremonial pardon. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump pardoned two turkeys named Freedom and Feathers Tuesday, a Thanksgiving White House tradition that dates back to the George H.W. Bush administration.
Trump used the brief event on the White House South Lawn to tout renovations, including a new granite helipad and progress on the ballroom, where he said next year’s turkeys will receive accommodations.
The two turkeys this year from West Virginia, presented by the trade group the National Turkey Federation, stayed in a suite at the nearby luxury Willard InterContinental Hotel.
“Unfortunately for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodations to host such distinguished guests. They’ve done this for a long time. We’ve saved a lot of turkeys, but I’m pleased to announce that next year we’ll be able to have a special location right over there,” Trump said, signaling to the construction site for a 90,000-square-foot ballroom where the East Wing stood.
Construction has continued after the U.S. Supreme Court stayed an injunction in August against further progress on the structure.
The modern White House turkey pardon began in 1989, according to the White House Historical Association. The tradition of presenting a turkey to the president began with President Harry Truman, the association says.
Trump acknowledged West Virginia farmers Scott and Becky Rightsell, who raised the turkeys on their farm in Pendleton County.
“We won West Virginia by 45 points. At least I did when I was on the ballot,” Trump said, inflating his margin in the 2024 presidential election. He defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris in the state by 41.9 percentage points, according to The Associated Press.
“I don’t know what the hell happened with this last election. Somebody, please explain it to me,” Trump said.
Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance have attributed the drubbing to the administration’s ongoing war with Iran, which significantly raised gas and diesel prices.
Outgoing U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., stood beside Trump as he delivered the traditional pardon. Johnson has announced he will not remain in House Republican leadership
